clue.text: Swamps with gold in great quantity

definitions.note: the clue gives a plural noun for a single word naming a boggy area

indicators.note: in tells us the word for gold sits inside the word for a great quantity

parts.note: a mass is a great quantity, as in masses of people
OR is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: Marshes rich in gold, lying around in vast amounts, sound like a prospector's dream.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is heraldry's word for gold. The definition is plural while the answer is singular, a looseness in the clue as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: A morass is a tract of boggy wet ground, a marsh or swamp.

clue.text: Suspicion of corrosion following condensation

indicators.note: following means the word for corrosion comes after the word for condensation

parts.note: mist is water condensed into fine droplets
rust is the corrosion of iron

explanation.surface: Someone suspects corrosion has set in after damp built up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts the corrosion word after the condensation word, the order in which the answer reads.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistrust is a lack of trust, a doubting or suspicious attitude.

clue.text: Welsh back out

explanation.surface: A Welsh person retreats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh' looks like the nationality, but to welsh is to fail to pay a debt or keep a promise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean going back on a promise or a bet; this is a less common spelling of renege.

clue.text: Yellow flower's fruit is under-weight

indicators.note: under, in a down clue, puts the word for fruit beneath the word for weight

parts.note: a stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds
a crop is the fruit or yield of the land

explanation.surface: A yellow bloom's fruit is too light.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'under-weight' is read as two words, so the fruit goes beneath the weight in this down entry. A stone is a British unit of fourteen pounds, still used for body weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Stonecrop is a sedum, a low succulent plant whose common wild kind bears yellow star-shaped blooms.

clue.text: Rousing game in the Netherlands…

explanation.surface: Some stirring sport is to be had in Holland, the clue trailing off into the next one.
explanation.walkthrough: To flush game is to drive birds from cover so they can be shot. Flushing (Vlissingen) is a port in the Netherlands; the dots carry the sentence on into 10 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Rousing birds from cover is what beaters do on a shoot, and the Dutch port Vlissingen is called by that name in English.

clue.text: Young conductors or principal violins? Both!

explanation.surface: Junior orchestra leaders or the top fiddles: the clue says it means both.
explanation.walkthrough: Leading strings were the reins once used to guide a toddler, so they conduct the young; principal violins are the leading players in the string section.
explanation.definitionFit: Toddlers' harness reins steer small children, and the front desks of the orchestra's violins head that section.

clue.text: Compress rubbish

explanation.surface: Crush the waste down.
explanation.definitionFit: To cram or pack tightly into something, and worthless material or nonsense.

clue.text: Jaundice? Cook cures it!

indicators.note: cook means the letters of the following words are doctored into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks about jaundice and is told that a chef will heal it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' is the anagram signal on CURES IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Icterus is the medical term for yellowing of the skin from excess bile pigment.

clue.text: Wine writer

explanation.surface: A drink and an author, two words side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the Bordeaux wine region and its wine; the other is Robert Graves, the poet and novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine from a district of Bordeaux, and Robert Graves, author of I, Claudius.

clue.text: Girth, say, of 800 metres

explanation.surface: A measurement around the waist is linked to a running event.
explanation.walkthrough: Girth is the distance round the middle; the 800 metres is a middle-distance race in athletics.
explanation.definitionFit: A waist measurement is a span around one's midriff, and the 800 metres is classed between sprints and long-distance running.

clue.text: …but a miss from Brazil is another problem

definitions.note: the Portuguese form of address for a young unmarried woman, used in Brazil

indicators.note: a problem leaves things in a mess, so the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: Continuing from the Dutch clue, a young woman from Brazil turns out to be yet another difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problem' is the anagram signal working on IS ANOTHER. 'Miss' here is a young unmarried woman, and Brazil speaks Portuguese.
explanation.definitionFit: Senhorita is the Portuguese title for an unmarried young woman, the equivalent of the English courtesy title for one.

clue.text: Extremist involved in awful tragedy

indicators.note: involved in signals letters wrapped up within the next two words

explanation.surface: A fanatic has played a part in a terrible disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' signals the run hidden across awfUL TRAgedy.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is a person holding extreme views, especially in politics.

clue.text: Horseplay and tobacco — known cause of 28

parts.note: a rag is a boisterous prank or piece of horseplay, as in a student rag
the weed is an old slang name for tobacco

explanation.surface: Rough games and smoking are blamed for an allergy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to 28 across, the allergy caused by pollen. In Britain a rag is also a students' charity carnival of pranks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragweed is a plant whose pollen is a notorious trigger of the allergy at 28 across.

clue.text: Effective, like a serving policeman

explanation.surface: Something valid is compared to an officer still on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase: a serving policeman is in the force, the police.
explanation.definitionFit: A law that is operative is said to be in operation, and a constable still serving is a member of the police service.

clue.text: Promise Sunday sport

parts.note: to sport a garment is to wear it

explanation.surface: Someone pledges to play games on the Sabbath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sport' looks like a noun for a game but is the verb meaning to show off clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To vow something solemnly is to give one's word under oath.

clue.text: Poisoning from Rye reported

parts.note: reads like a news item from the Sussex town of Rye, but describes the illness caused by eating grain infected with a fungus

explanation.surface: A news report tells of a poisoning case in the town of Rye.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised Rye suggests the Sussex town; the real rye is the cereal, whose fungal infection causes the illness.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition comes from eating bread made with cereal infected by a fungus that grows on the grain.

clue.text: Tinker wandering in, effort to, make baubles

indicators.note: wandering means the letters of the word for a travelling mender stray into a new order

parts.note: a try is an attempt or effort

explanation.surface: A travelling mender roams around trying to make cheap ornaments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering' rearranges the six letters of the travelling mender, giving the first six letters of the answer before the effort word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trinketry means trinkets collectively, cheap showy ornaments.

clue.text: Trawl — and catch nothing but spiny fish

parts.note: to drag a net along the sea bed is to trawl
O looks like zero, nothing
to net a fish is to catch it

explanation.surface: A trawlerman drags the sea and lands only a prickly fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring for nothing sits between the trawl and the catch, though the clue mentions catch before nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragonet is a small bottom-dwelling sea fish with spines on its gill covers and fins.

clue.text: Hands may be high here, at end of barrel

definitions.text: Hands may be high here, at end of barrel

parts.words: Hands may be high here, at end of barrel
parts.note: describes being held up by a robber with a firearm: arms raised, facing the business end of the weapon

explanation.surface: A scene of people raising their hands while threatened by a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Hold-up victims put their hands up when threatened; 'barrel' might suggest a cask, but it is the tube of a firearm, whose tip is its point.
explanation.definitionFit: Being held at the tip of a firearm makes victims raise their hands in surrender.

clue.text: Lifting your head continually for this makes you golf badly

definitions.text: Lifting your head continually for this

indicators.note: badly signals that the two words before it are played out of order

explanation.surface: Golfing advice: keep looking up and your game will suffer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges YOU GOLF. Golfers are told not to lift their heads, but in the definition the head lifts to scan the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Ufology is the study of unidentified flying objects, which means constantly watching the sky.

clue.text: Nitre processed in Hulme, you could say

definitions.note: spoken aloud, in Hulme sounds like inhume, meaning to bury

indicators.note: processed means the letters of the chemical word are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Saltpetre is being treated in Hulme, a district of Manchester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'processed' rearranges NITRE. Hulme is an area of Manchester; said aloud it sounds like inhume, to bury, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To inhume is to bury a body, the same as committing it to a grave.

clue.text: Fatty not hot in ripped old hat

indicators.note: in means the shortened word goes inside the word for ripped

parts.note: torn means ripped

indicators.note: not means the letter for hot is dropped from the word for fatty

parts.note: rich food is fatty
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A fat person, not overheated, wears a torn antique hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' takes the hot letter out of the word for fatty, and 'in' slips the three letters left inside the word for ripped.
explanation.definitionFit: A tricorn is a three-cornered hat of the eighteenth century, an old style of headwear.

clue.text: Prominently-printed sensation that weakens the spirit

explanation.surface: A headline story about something that dilutes liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: A splash is a big front-page news story; a splash of water also dilutes whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A front-page story given bold display, and a small dash of water added to spirits.

clue.text: Complain and curse about, corruption

indicators.note: about means the word for a curse goes around the word for corruption

parts.note: a pest is a nuisance or plague, a curse
rot is decay or corruption

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles and swears about dishonesty in high places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curse' looks like a verb meaning to swear but is a noun, a plague or nuisance; 'about' wraps it round the decay.
explanation.definitionFit: To object or grumble publicly is to raise an objection, a formal expression of disapproval.

clue.text: End of the lake is ghostly

indicators.note: End of picks the last letter of the word that follows

parts.note: Erie is one of the Great Lakes

explanation.surface: The far shore of a lake is spooky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' takes E from 'the', then ERIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means strange and frightening, uncanny like a haunting.

clue.text: Slight hint of blackening around opening of lamp

indicators.note: around means the word for blackening encloses the letter that follows

parts.note: inking is blackening with ink

indicators.note: opening of picks out the first letter of the word lamp

explanation.surface: A lamp's first flicker gives a faint suggestion of darkening soot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' places L, the opening of 'lamp', inside INKING.
explanation.definitionFit: An inkling is a vague notion or faint suspicion of something.

clue.text: Affair of a doctor taking half an hour

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor

indicators.note: half means only the second half of the word hour is taken

explanation.surface: A physician spends thirty minutes on a romantic fling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes the back half of 'hour', UR. MO is a medical officer, an army doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: An amour is a love affair, often a secret one.

clue.text: Urban nurseryman's late shift?

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme figure who runs through the town at bedtime is in his nightclothes; a shift is a loose garment, not a work period

explanation.surface: A city gardener working a night rota.
explanation.walkthrough: Wee Willie Winkie runs through the town upstairs and downstairs in his nightgown: the nurseryman is a nursery-rhyme man, and a shift is a simple dress or slip.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose garment worn in bed, which the rhyme's town-runner wears late at night.

clue.text: Noel's pollinosis?

explanation.surface: Someone's allergy to pollen is attributed to Noel.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward wrote a comic play of this name; pollinosis is the medical term for the allergy to pollen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Coward comedy about the Bliss family shares its title with the common seasonal allergy to pollen.

clue.text: Sound sort of ring for a young bard?

indicators.note: Sound tells us the word for the ring is said aloud and spelt another way

parts.note: a signet is a ring bearing a seal

explanation.surface: Someone asks what kind of ring would suit a junior poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare is the Swan of Avon, so a bard is a swan and a young one is a baby swan.
explanation.definitionFit: A poet like Shakespeare is called the Swan of Avon, so a young bard is a baby swan.
